title: Codecs
subheading: Lossy vs lossless, audio codecs and containers explained.

contents.Text: [[[strong:Lossy codecs]]] compress audio by discarding some of the data. This gives [[[strong:smaller files]]], but with [[[strong:reduced quality]]]. [[[warning:Lossy]]]
[[[strong:Lossless codecs]]] keep all of the original audio data. This gives the [[[strong:best quality]]], but at the cost of [[[strong:larger files]]]. [[[warning:Lossless]]]

[[[warning:Note:]]] Converting a [[[strong:lossy]]] file to a [[[strong:lossless]]] format does not bring the quality back, as the discarded data is gone for good. Sites such as [[[strong:YouTube]]] serve [[[strong:lossy]]] audio, so a [[[strong:lossless]]] codec cannot improve on the [[[strong:source]]]. It only makes the files [[[strong:bigger]]].

[[[warning:Note:]]] Converting from one [[[strong:lossy]]] codec to another, for example [[[strong:MP3]]] to [[[strong:Opus]]], loses a little more quality each time. Avoid [[[strong:re-encoding]]] lossy files where you can.
•[[[warning:Lossy]]] - Smaller files, with some quality removed.
•[[[warning:Lossless]]] - Larger files, with no quality removed.
•[[[strong:Recommended]]] - The codecs I suggest you use.
•[[[italics:Container]]] - A file wrapper rather than a codec. See [[[strong:Containers]]] below.
•[[[italics:Transparent]]] - Most people cannot tell the file apart from the original in a blind test.
[[[strong:Just want it to work?]]] Choose [[[strong:Opus]]]. [[[strong:Want the best possible quality?]]] Choose [[[strong:FLAC]]].

Rarely worth it, as FLAC is far smaller

contents.Text: [[[warning:Note:]]] Sizes are approximate and are for a 4-minute song. See each codec below for more detail.

[[[strong:Bitrate]]] is how much data is used for each second of audio, measured in [[[strong:kbps]]] (kilobits per second). A [[[strong:higher bitrate]]] gives better quality, up to a point, and a [[[strong:bigger file]]].

RhythmiRust has [[[strong:no bitrate or quality setting]]], but you can see the bitrate of any downloaded song in the [[[strong:metadata editor]]]. The guidance on this page tells you what those numbers mean.
•[[[strong:Diminishing returns:]]] Once a codec sounds [[[italics:transparent]]], a higher bitrate only makes the file bigger.

•[[[strong:Not comparable between codecs:]]] A newer codec can match an older one at a lower bitrate. In public listening tests, [[[strong:Opus]]] at [[[strong:96 kbps]]] was rated as good as or better than [[[strong:MP3]]] at around [[[strong:128 to 140 kbps]]].

•[[[strong:VBR and CBR:]]] [[[strong:CBR]]] (constant bitrate) uses the same bitrate throughout. [[[strong:VBR]]] (variable bitrate) adjusts it to suit the music, and usually gives better quality for the same file size.

contents.Header3: Your download is limited by its source

contents.Text: A download can never sound better than the [[[strong:source]]] it came from, and a [[[strong:higher bitrate]]] or a [[[strong:lossless]]] codec cannot change that. Typical source quality:
•[[[strong:YouTube]]] - AAC at about [[[strong:128 kbps]]], or Opus at about [[[strong:130 to 160 kbps]]]. The exact figure varies from video to video.
•[[[strong:SoundCloud]]] - Standard streams are roughly [[[strong:64 to 160 kbps]]], depending on the format used, with [[[strong:AAC]]] at [[[strong:160 kbps]]] usually the best on offer.
[[[strong:Tip:]]] [[[strong:YouTube]]]'s best audio is usually [[[strong:Opus]]], so choosing Opus is a natural match and avoids converting from one lossy codec to another where possible.
•[[[strong:WAV]]] [[[warning:Lossless]]] - About [[[strong:42 MB]]] (1,411 kbps at CD quality).
•[[[strong:FLAC]]] [[[warning:Lossless]]] - About [[[strong:21 to 25 MB]]] (typically 50 to 60% of the WAV size), or up to about 30 MB for dense, loud music.
•[[[strong:ALAC]]] [[[warning:Lossless]]] - Similar to FLAC, often a little larger.
•[[[strong:Lossy at 320 kbps]]] - About [[[strong:9.6 MB]]] (23% of WAV).
•[[[strong:Lossy at 256 kbps]]] - About [[[strong:7.7 MB]]] (18% of WAV).
•[[[strong:Lossy at 192 kbps]]] - About [[[strong:5.8 MB]]] (14% of WAV).
•[[[strong:Lossy at 128 kbps]]] - About [[[strong:3.8 MB]]] (9% of WAV).
•[[[strong:Lossy at 96 kbps]]] - About [[[strong:2.9 MB]]] (7% of WAV).

[[[warning:Note:]]] Lossy sizes are worked out from the [[[strong:bitrate]]] (bitrate multiplied by length), so [[[strong:VBR]]] files will vary slightly. [[[strong:Lossless]]] sizes depend on the music, as quiet or simple tracks compress better than dense ones.
You choose the [[[strong:codec]]] when adding a category in the [[[button:Playlist Editor][/Main Window/Downloader/Playlist Editor]]].
•[[[strong:Type:]]] [[[warning:Lossy]]]
•[[[strong:Recommended:]]] Small files with great quality.

A modern codec with an excellent [[[strong:quality-to-size ratio]]], and support for [[[strong:variable bitrates]]]. It is one of the most [[[strong:efficient]]] lossy codecs available, and is generally at its strongest at [[[strong:low to medium bitrates]]].

•[[[strong:Good bitrate:]]] [[[strong:96 kbps]]] or higher is good for music, and around [[[strong:128 kbps]]] is close to [[[italics:transparent]]] for most listeners. Going higher has little benefit. A 4-minute song at 128 kbps is about [[[strong:3.8 MB]]].
[[[warning:Note:]]] Opus is finally natively supported by RhythmiRust as of version [[[strong:0.4.0]]], so no fallback decoder is needed when playing it.
•[[[strong:Type:]]] [[[warning:Lossless]]]
•[[[strong:Recommended:]]] The best possible quality, for example for archiving.

The [[[strong:Free Lossless Audio Codec]]]. An [[[strong:open]]] and widely supported codec for audiophile-grade music. Files are smaller than [[[strong:WAV]]] with no loss of quality, and [[[strong:tags]]] and [[[strong:cover art]]] are well supported.

•[[[strong:File size:]]] Typically around [[[strong:50 to 60%]]] of the WAV size, and up to about 70% for dense music. That is roughly [[[strong:700 to 1,000 kbps]]] in the metadata editor. A 4-minute CD-quality song is about [[[strong:21 to 30 MB]]].
•[[[strong:Type:]]] [[[warning:Lossy]]]
[[[strong:Advanced Audio Coding]]]. It gives [[[strong:better quality than MP3]]] at a similar file size and is widely supported, particularly on [[[strong:Apple]]] devices.

•[[[strong:Good bitrate:]]] Around [[[strong:128 kbps]]] is a good balance of size and quality, and [[[strong:192 to 256 kbps]]] is very high quality. [[[strong:256 kbps]]] is what Apple uses for its iTunes Store downloads.
•[[[strong:Tip:]]] AAC is usually stored inside an [[[strong:M4A]]] container.
•[[[strong:Type:]]] [[[warning:Lossy]]]
The classic lossy codec. It plays on almost anything, but it is [[[strong:dated]]], and [[[strong:Opus]]] and [[[strong:AAC]]] give better quality at the same file size.

•[[[strong:Good bitrate:]]] Around [[[strong:190 to 256 kbps]]] is generally [[[italics:transparent]]]. [[[strong:128 kbps]]] is a noticeable step down for many listeners, and [[[strong:320 kbps]]] is not meaningfully better than [[[strong:256 kbps]]], with larger files.
•[[[strong:Tip:]]] Only choose MP3 if you need compatibility with an older player.
•[[[strong:Type:]]] [[[warning:Lossy]]]
An [[[strong:open-source]]] lossy codec with good quality at [[[strong:low bitrates]]]. [[[strong:Opus]]] is its modern successor.
•[[[strong:Good bitrate:]]] Around [[[strong:128 to 192 kbps]]]. About [[[strong:160 kbps]]] is the usual choice for near-CD quality.
•[[[strong:Tip:]]] Opus is more efficient, so prefer Opus unless you specifically need Vorbis.
•[[[strong:Type:]]] [[[warning:Lossless]]]

The [[[strong:Apple Lossless Audio Codec]]]. It gives the same quality as [[[strong:FLAC]]], but is mainly used within [[[strong:Apple's]]] ecosystem. It is usually stored inside an [[[strong:M4A]]] container.
•[[[strong:File size:]]] Similar to FLAC, but often a few percentage points larger.
•[[[strong:Tip:]]] Unless you specifically need ALAC for Apple devices, FLAC is the better choice.
•[[[strong:Type:]]] [[[warning:Lossless]]]
Usually [[[strong:uncompressed]]] audio, giving the highest possible quality at the cost of [[[strong:very large files]]]. [[[strong:Tag support is limited.]]]

•[[[strong:File size:]]] CD quality (44.1 kHz, 16-bit, stereo) is [[[strong:1,411 kbps]]], which is about [[[strong:10.6 MB]]] per minute. High-resolution audio at 96 kHz and 24-bit is [[[strong:4,608 kbps]]], or about [[[strong:34.6 MB]]] per minute.
[[[warning:Note:]]] WAV files are far larger than [[[strong:FLAC]]] with no quality benefit, so they are rarely worth choosing for a music library.
•[[[strong:Type:]]] [[[italics:Container]]]

A [[[strong:container]]] rather than a codec, made popular by Apple and now widely supported. It usually holds [[[strong:AAC]]] [[[warning:Lossy]]] or [[[strong:ALAC]]] [[[warning:Lossless]]], so the quality depends on what is inside.
[[[warning:Note:]]] M4A is supported by RhythmiRust. It simply uses the decoder for the codec inside, so AAC and ALAC files play as normal.

A [[[strong:codec]]] decides how the audio is compressed. A [[[strong:container]]] is the file wrapper that holds the encoded audio, along with extras such as [[[strong:tags]]] and [[[strong:cover art]]].
Think of the codec as how the audio is packed, and the container as the box it is packed in.
•[[[strong:.m4a]]] - An MPEG-4 container. Holds [[[strong:AAC]]] or [[[strong:ALAC]]].
•[[[strong:.ogg]]] - An Ogg container. Usually holds [[[strong:Vorbis]]], but can also hold [[[strong:Opus]]].
•[[[strong:.opus]]] - [[[strong:Opus]]] audio in an Ogg container.
•[[[strong:.flac]]] - [[[strong:FLAC]]] audio in its own native file format.
•[[[strong:.mp3]]] - [[[strong:MP3]]] audio. The codec and the file format share the same name.
•[[[strong:.wav]]] - Usually holds [[[strong:uncompressed]]] audio.

[[[warning:Note:]]] The file extension only tells you the container. The codec inside decides whether the audio is [[[strong:lossy]]] or [[[strong:lossless]]], so an [[[strong:.m4a]]] file can be either.

[[[strong:Metadata]]] is the information stored inside an audio file, such as the title, artist, album, genre, track number and [[[strong:cover art]]]. It lets a player display and sort your music properly, without relying on file names.
Each format stores its tags in its own way:
•[[[strong:ID3]]] - Used by [[[strong:MP3]]] files.
•[[[strong:Vorbis comments]]] - Used by [[[strong:FLAC]]], [[[strong:Ogg Vorbis]]] and [[[strong:Opus]]] files.
•[[[strong:MP4 tags]]] - Used by [[[strong:M4A]]] files (AAC and ALAC).
•[[[strong:RIFF INFO]]] - Used by [[[strong:WAV]]] files. Support is limited.
[[[strong:Tip:]]] Tags are stored inside the file, so they stay with it when you move or rename it.
[[[warning:Note:]]] [[[strong:WAV]]] has the weakest tag support of all, so it is the poorest choice if you care about your tags.
•[[[button:Metadata Formats (Technical)][/_Guides/Metadata Formats (Technical)]]] - Each tag format explained in detail.
•[[[strong:Opus]]] [[[warning:Lossy]]] [[[strong:Recommended]]] - Small files with great quality.
•[[[strong:FLAC]]] [[[warning:Lossless]]] [[[strong:Recommended]]] - The best quality, with larger files.
Only pick another codec if you have a specific reason to, such as compatibility with an older player or Apple devices.
Check the [[[strong:bitrate]]] in the metadata editor after a download:
•[[[strong:Opus]]] - [[[strong:96 kbps]]] or higher, with around [[[strong:128 kbps]]] close to transparent.
•[[[strong:AAC]]] - Around [[[strong:128 kbps]]] is good, and [[[strong:192 to 256 kbps]]] is very high quality.
•[[[strong:MP3]]] - Around [[[strong:190 to 256 kbps]]].
•[[[strong:Vorbis]]] - Around [[[strong:128 to 192 kbps]]].
•[[[strong:FLAC, ALAC and WAV]]] - Lossless, so there is no quality to judge from the bitrate.
[[[warning:Note:]]] These are guides, not rules. Quality depends on the music, the encoder and your listening equipment, and a download can never be better than its [[[strong:source]]].
